_note: Original lessons. Exercise types: mcq (answer = option index), fill (answer = accepted strings), fix (find the error: answer = index of the wrong word in tokens, plus correction).

lessons.title: Present simple
lessons.summary: Use the present simple for facts, habits and routines.

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.text: Facts that are always true, and things that happen regularly.

sections.heading: He / she / it + -s
sections.text: Add -s (or -es) to the verb after he, she, it or a single person or thing.

sections.heading: Questions and negatives
sections.text: Use do / does + the base verb. After does, the verb has no -s.

mistakes: After does, use the base verb.

exercises.prompt: My brother ___ in London.
___ you speak Spanish?
She ___ (not / like) spicy food.
exercises.explanation: Negative with she: doesn't + base verb.

exercises.prompt: The train ___ at 7:30 every day.
exercises.explanation: Timetables and routines use the present simple; the train = it → leaves.

exercises.prompt: Where ___ your parents live?
Find the mistake: He go to school by bus.

lessons.title: Past simple
lessons.summary: Talk about finished actions at a specific time in the past.

sections.heading: Regular verbs
sections.text: Add -ed: work → worked, study → studied, stop → stopped.

sections.heading: Irregular verbs
sections.text: Many common verbs are irregular and must be learned.

sections.heading: Questions and negatives
sections.text: Use did / didn't + the base verb.

mistakes: After didn't, use the base verb.

exercises.prompt: Last summer we ___ to Italy.
She ___ (study) medicine at university.
___ you finish your homework?
I ___ (not / see) him at the party.
They ___ the bus because they were late.
Find the mistake: Did she called you yesterday?
exercises.explanation: After did, use the base verb: call.

lessons.title: Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.summary: Compare two things (bigger, more expensive) or one with all others (the biggest).

sections.heading: Short adjectives
sections.text: Add -er / -est. Double the last letter after a short vowel.

sections.heading: Long adjectives
sections.text: Use more / the most with adjectives of two or more syllables (except -y).
examples: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive

sections.heading: Irregular
sections.text: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → further → the furthest
examples: This is the best book I have read.

mistakes: She is more tall than me.

exercises.prompt: My flat is ___ than yours.
This is the ___ film I’ve ever seen.
Gold is ___ (expensive) than silver.
Today is the ___ (hot) day of the year.
Your English is getting ___.
Find the mistake: The exam was more easier than I expected.

lessons.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
lessons.summary: Some nouns can be counted (books), others can’t (information). This changes the words you use with them.

sections.heading: Countable
sections.text: Singular and plural forms; use a/an, many, a few.

sections.heading: Uncountable
sections.text: No plural, no a/an; use much, a little, some.

mistakes: How many money do you have?
How much money do you have?

exercises.prompt: Can you give me some ___ about the course?
There aren’t ___ people here today.
How ___ homework do you have tonight?
We bought new ___ for the living room.
I only need a ___ sugar in my tea.
Find the mistake: The researchers published many researches last year.
exercises.explanation: Research is uncountable. Use ‘a lot of research’ or ‘many studies’.

lessons.title: Present perfect vs past simple
lessons.summary: Use the present perfect for experiences and past actions connected to now; use the past simple for finished times.

sections.heading: Present perfect: have/has + past participle
sections.text: Experiences (ever, never), changes, and situations continuing to now (for, since).

sections.heading: Past simple
sections.text: A finished time is mentioned or clear (yesterday, in 2018, last week, when I was a child).

sections.heading: For and since
sections.text: for + a period (for three years); since + a starting point (since Monday).
examples: I've known her for ten years.
We've been here since nine o'clock.

exercises.prompt: I ___ that film three times.
exercises.explanation: Experience, no finished time: have seen.

exercises.prompt: We ___ to Paris in 2015.
She has worked here ___ five years.
They have been married ___ 2010.
___ you ever ___ sushi?
exercises.explanation: Experience question: Have you ever eaten…?

exercises.prompt: Find the mistake: I have finished my essay last night.
exercises.explanation: Last night is a finished time → past simple.

lessons.title: First and second conditionals
lessons.summary: Talk about real possibilities (first) and imaginary or unlikely situations (second).

sections.heading: First conditional
sections.text: If + present simple, will + verb. For real, likely future situations.
examples: If it rains, we will stay inside.
I'll call you if I finish early.

sections.heading: Second conditional
sections.text: If + past simple, would + verb. For imaginary or unlikely situations now or in the future.
examples: If I had more time, I would learn the guitar.
If I were you, I would apologise.

mistakes: If it will rain, we'll stay home.
If it rains, we'll stay home.
If I would have money, I would travel.
If I had money, I would travel.

exercises.prompt: If you heat ice, it ___.
If I ___ rich, I would buy a house by the sea.
If she studies hard, she ___ (pass) the exam.
What ___ you do if you lost your phone?
I ___ you if I hear any news.
Find the mistake: If it will be sunny tomorrow, we will have a picnic.
exercises.explanation: Use present simple after if, not will.

lessons.title: The passive voice
lessons.summary: Use the passive when the action is more important than who did it. Very common in IELTS Writing Task 1 processes.

sections.heading: Form: be + past participle
sections.text: The tense is shown by ‘be’.
examples: The results will be announced tomorrow.

sections.heading: Saying who did it
sections.text: Add by + person only when it’s useful.
examples: The novel was written by a teenager.

sections.heading: Describing processes
sections.text: Use the present passive with sequencing words.
examples: First, the beans are picked. Then they are dried in the sun.

exercises.prompt: English ___ in many countries.
The windows ___ (clean) every week.
The criminals ___ last night.
After cutting, the wood ___ (transport) to the factory.
A new hospital ___ next year.
Find the mistake: The data were collect from 500 students.

lessons.title: Modals for advice and obligation
lessons.summary: should, must, have to, don’t have to, mustn’t — and the difference between them.

sections.heading: Advice
sections.text: should / ought to + verb.
examples: Governments ought to invest in schools.

sections.heading: Obligation
sections.text: must (the speaker's opinion or rules), have to (external rules).
examples: We have to wear a uniform at work.

sections.heading: No obligation vs prohibition
sections.text: don’t have to = it’s not necessary; mustn’t = it’s not allowed.
examples: You don't have to come — it's optional.

mistakes: You should to see a doctor.
You don't have to pay; it's free.

exercises.prompt: You ___ wear a seatbelt. It’s the law.
It’s Sunday, so I ___ get up early.
You ___ touch that wire — it’s dangerous!
I think you ___ apologise to her. (advice)
Students ___ submit essays before Friday.
Find the mistake: You should to practise every day.

lessons.title: Relative clauses
lessons.summary: Join ideas with who, which, that, whose, where, when — and use commas correctly.

sections.heading: Defining clauses (no commas)
sections.text: Identify which person or thing we mean. ‘That’ is possible.
examples: The woman who/that lives next door is a doctor.
The book that I lent you is overdue.

sections.heading: Non-defining clauses (commas)
sections.text: Add extra information. Don’t use ‘that’.
examples: My sister, who lives in Dhaka, is a teacher.
The Nile, which is the longest river in Africa, flows north.

sections.heading: Whose, where, when
sections.text: whose = possession; where = place; when = time.
examples: The student whose bag was stolen called the police.
This is the café where we met.
I remember the day when we arrived.

mistakes: My father, that is a pilot, travels a lot.
My father, who is a pilot, travels a lot.
The man which called you is here.
The man who called you is here.

exercises.prompt: The scientist ___ discovered penicillin was Alexander Fleming.
That’s the town ___ I grew up.
The company, ___ was founded in 1990, employs 500 people.
I know a man ___ car runs on electricity.
Do you remember the year ___ we first met?
Find the mistake: London, that is the capital of the UK, is very expensive.

lessons.title: Third and mixed conditionals
lessons.summary: Talk about imaginary past situations and their results.

sections.heading: Third conditional
sections.text: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. The past cannot change.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed.
She wouldn't have missed the flight if she had left earlier.

sections.heading: Mixed conditional
sections.text: Imaginary past cause → present result: If + past perfect, would + verb.
examples: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.

mistakes: If I would have known, I would have helped.
If I had known, I would have helped.

exercises.prompt: If we ___ the map, we wouldn’t have got lost.
If she had asked me, I ___ (help) her.
If I hadn’t moved abroad, I ___ English so well now.
exercises.explanation: Mixed: past cause, present result → would + verb.

exercises.prompt: He would have won if he ___ so tired.
If they ___ (not / cancel) the concert, we would have gone.
Find the mistake: If I would have seen you, I would have said hello.
exercises.explanation: Use the past perfect after if.

lessons.title: Articles: a, an, the or nothing
lessons.summary: One of the most common errors in IELTS writing. Learn the core rules.

sections.heading: a / an
sections.text: First mention of a singular countable noun, or ‘one of many’.

sections.heading: the
sections.text: Something specific or already known, unique things, superlatives, and some place names.

sections.heading: No article
sections.text: General statements with plural or uncountable nouns.

mistakes: The pollution is a big problem in cities.
Pollution is a big problem in cities.
She is best student in class.
She is the best student in the class.

exercises.prompt: ___ education is important for everyone.
I bought ___ umbrella yesterday.
___ moon goes round the Earth.
He wants to become ___ engineer.
exercises.explanation: Jobs: a/an. Vowel sound: an engineer.

exercises.prompt: Mount Everest is ___ highest mountain in the world.
Find the mistake: The technology has changed the way we work.

lessons.title: Gerunds and infinitives
lessons.summary: Some verbs are followed by -ing, others by to + verb.

sections.heading: Verb + -ing
sections.text: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, consider, keep, practise.

sections.heading: Verb + to + verb
sections.text: want, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse, manage, afford.

sections.heading: After prepositions: -ing
sections.text: Always use -ing after a preposition.

exercises.prompt: Would you mind ___ the window?
They can’t afford ___ a new car.
I’m looking forward to ___ (see) you.
He managed ___ the exam despite being ill.
She is good at ___ (solve) problems.
Find the mistake: I suggest to start the meeting earlier.

lessons.title: Reported speech
lessons.summary: Report what someone said, usually moving the tense one step back.

sections.heading: Tense backshift
sections.text: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could.
examples: “I'm tired.” → She said she was tired.
“I will help.” → He said he would help.

sections.heading: Questions
sections.text: Use statement word order; use if/whether for yes/no questions.
examples: “Where do you live?” → He asked where I lived.
“Are you ready?” → She asked if I was ready.

sections.heading: Say vs tell
sections.text: tell + person; say (to someone).
examples: She told me (that) she was busy.

mistakes: He asked me where did I live.
He asked me where I lived.
She said me she was late.
She told me she was late.

exercises.prompt: “I like jazz,” he said. → He said he ___ jazz.
She asked me ___ hungry.
“We will call you.” → They said they ___ call me.
My teacher ___ me to practise more.
“Where is the station?” → He asked where the station ___.
Find the mistake: She asked me what time did the film start.
exercises.explanation: No question word order in reported questions.

lessons.title: Hedging and cautious language
lessons.summary: Academic writers avoid overgeneralising. Hedging makes your claims more precise and convincing.

sections.heading: Modal verbs
sections.text: may, might, could, tend to.
examples: This may lead to higher costs.
Young people tend to use social media more.

sections.heading: Adverbs and phrases
sections.text: arguably, possibly, largely, to some extent, in many cases.
examples: This is arguably the most serious problem.
The policy has been largely successful.

sections.heading: Avoid absolute words
sections.text: Replace always/never/everyone/all with often/rarely/most/many where the evidence is not absolute.
examples: All teenagers are addicted to phones. → Many teenagers spend several hours a day on their phones.

mistakes: Technology can make some people feel lonely.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is best for an IELTS essay?
options: Many people find public transport inconvenient.
Public transport is the worst thing ever.

exercises.prompt: Higher taxes ___ reduce smoking rates.
Older people ___ to prefer traditional media. (tend)
exercises.explanation: ‘Tend to’ shows a general pattern, not a rule.

exercises.prompt: The scheme has been ___ successful, although some problems remain.
exercises.explanation: Largely = mostly, leaving room for exceptions.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most academic option: ‘___, the main cause is poverty.’
Find the overgeneralisation: Children never read books these days.

lessons.title: Inversion for emphasis
lessons.summary: After negative or limiting adverbials at the start of a sentence, use question word order.

sections.heading: Negative adverbials
sections.text: Never, Rarely, Seldom, Not only, Under no circumstances, Little.
examples: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.

sections.heading: Time expressions
sections.text: Hardly / Scarcely … when; No sooner … than.
examples: No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.
Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.

sections.heading: Conditionals without if
sections.text: Had / Were / Should at the start.
examples: Had I known, I would have come.
Should you need help, please call.

exercises.prompt: Rarely ___ such dedication in a student.
Not only ___ late, but he also forgot his notes.
No sooner ___ I closed the door than the bell rang.
___ you require further information, please contact us.
___ I known about the problem, I would have helped.
exercises.explanation: Had I known = If I had known.

exercises.prompt: Find the mistake: Under no circumstances you should share your password.
exercises.explanation: Inversion: Under no circumstances should you…
